doc.title: Joel Dorn interviewed by Monk Rowe, New York City, New York, January 13, 2007

title: Making real records with jazz artists rather than jazz productions
summary: Dorn says he is a record producer, not a jazz producer, and describes working with Rahsaan, Yusef, Fathead, Les McCann and Eddie Harris. His heroes were Lieber and Stoller, Spector and George Martin.

story.theme_name: Teaching jazz: schools, students and advice to the young

blocks.x: When you said I’ve got some new ideas, you take an artist who’s already established or semi-established, what kind of ideas would you present to that artist?

Well I’ll give you a couple of real examples but when I say I had new ideas like everybody who wants to be a record producer says well here’s how I would record this person and that person. Jazz is not the only music I like, I’m not a jazz producer. I have worked with a lot of jazz artists. I’m a record producer. One of the things I got criticized for, and one of the things that made me successful on those Atlantic years, the same thing, was I took people like Rahsaan and Yusef and Les McCann and Eddie Harris — I want to say this right because I don’t want it to sound patronizing or condescending. There are a lot of people who can record a great jazz quintet or a trio or a sextet or a big band. I wasn’t interested in that kind of jazz production. I was interested in producing records with jazz artists. So I don’t know if you’re familiar with any of the Atlantic things, you know, that I did, but I would take Yusef, I would take Rahsaan, I would take Fathead, Les McCann and Eddie Harris especially, and we’d make what I want to say is real records. My biggest influences as producers, I mean I love what Nesuhi did, I love what John Hammond did, I love what Alfred Lion did and Orrin Keepnews and you know, Norman Granz, all the great jazz producers. But they were jazz producers. They rarely if ever stepped out of that mold or stepped out of that part of the music business. My heroes were Lieber and Stoller and Spector and then later on George Martin’s work only with The Beatles. And Allen Toussaint in New Orleans, and people like that. So what I wanted to do was make what I call real records but with jazz musicians. So I did that.
